subtitle_zh: Trish Spurlin 复盘 Babson 捐赠基金如何从小资金池集中押注风投、做到 25% 私募配置

With your host, Alexa Bans. And Ernest, you ready? Let's dive in. Welcome to our next guest on Swimming with Alligators.
turns.zh: 除了泰坦尼克号之外的任何船。等等等等，我是不是漏了什么？最后到底发生了什么？欢迎收听 Swimming with Allocators，一档从 LP（有限合伙人）视角出发的 VC（风险投资）播客，由你们的主持 Alexa Binns 带来。Earnest，你准备好了吗？我们下水吧。欢迎今天做客 Swimming with Allocators 的下一位嘉宾。

turns.en: This is Trish Spurlin at the Babson College Endowment. Hi, Trish. Hi, guys. Thanks so much for having me. Trish is overseeing a really remarkable endowment. The narrative behind the story of how they developed their venture back. Their venture heavy portfolio is really fascinating. We're excited to hear your story, Trish.
turns.zh: 这位是 Babson College Endowment 的 Trish Spurlin。Trish 你好。大家好，非常感谢你们邀请我。Trish 管理着一个非常了不起的捐赠基金（endowment）。他们是如何打造出这个偏重风险投资（venture）的组合的，这背后的故事非常有意思。我们很期待听你讲讲，Trish。

turns.en: And the story of the endowment that you're now in charge of. Thank you. I'm so excited to talk about it. Thank you. Most folks have... I don't want to say a clear path to their role managing something like a large endowment. But your story is so special.
turns.zh: 还有你现在掌管的这个捐赠基金本身的故事。谢谢，我特别期待聊这个。谢谢。大多数人……我不想说他们走上管理大型捐赠基金这类岗位的路径有多清晰，但你的经历真的很特别。

turns.en: Do you mind just giving us a little bit of your narrative of how you got to where you are? Sure. Definitely not the traditional path, I would say. Okay. So I really went to college. I would say originally to play lacrosse. I had no idea what I was going to do. At one point I was going to be an athletic trainer.
turns.zh: 你介意先给我们讲讲你自己是怎么一路走到今天的吗？当然，我会说这绝对不是一条传统路径。好。说实话我当初上大学，主要是为了打长曲棍球（lacrosse）。我完全不知道自己以后要做什么。有一阵子我还打算当运动防护师（athletic trainer）。

turns.en: But I'm really afraid of blood and really squeamish. So that was a great fit. And then I just sort of like bumbled around until I found accounting and finance. I was doing well in those classes. And they said I'd be able to get a job. So that's really how I ended up in the finance industry. It's like what everyone dreams of, right?
turns.zh: 但我特别怕血，还特别容易晕，所以那真是个“绝配”。后来我就一路瞎摸瞎撞，直到碰上会计和金融。这两类课我成绩不错，而且他们说这个能找到工作。所以我就是这么进入金融行业的——这可是所有人梦想的路径，对吧？

turns.en: And so when I graduated, I could either go to the accounting or the finance route. I chose to go accounting because they didn't want to move to New York. I later learned that there's like a lot of finance jobs that don't require you to move to New York. But that was my approach.
turns.zh: 所以毕业的时候，我要么走会计路线，要么走金融路线。我选了会计，因为我不想搬去 New York。后来我才知道，其实有很多金融工作并不需要你搬去 New York。但当时我就是这么想的。

turns.en: So I worked in accounting and public accounting for about three years. I kept getting feedback that maybe it wasn't like a great fit for my personality. Yeah, I was saying you went into accounting and I have not fell asleep yet. Wait, what is that? Like review? Like your annual review? They're like you? You talk a lot more than I.
turns.zh: 我在会计行业、在会计师事务所干了大概三年。我一直收到的反馈是，这工作可能跟我的性格不太合。是啊，我正想说呢，你进了会计行业，而我居然还没睡着。等等，那是什么？绩效评估？你的年度评估？他们是这么写你的？“你话比我多多了”。

turns.en: It was more you talk a lot. That was sort of your debt on. I think like I, my job in the audit room was like no one wanted to talk to the client. And they would be like oh, we'll send trash. Like that was sort of my role. And what ended up happening, which is like very critical to how I got here, is they sort of pushed me into tech.
turns.zh: 更准确说是“你话太多”，那算是你的招牌特点。我觉得我在审计室里的角色就是——没人愿意跟客户聊天，他们就会说“哦，那就派 Trish 去”。这大概就是我的定位。而后来发生的一件事，对我走到今天非常关键：他们把我推去了科技组。

turns.en: They were like this is sort of this evolving category. The rules around accounting are very ambiguous. So we need people who are comfortable with like operating without a set of accounting principles basically. And so they sent me over. I was at this. You need somebody to move money in your book or go to church. Sounds terrible.
turns.zh: 他们说这是一个还在演变中的领域，会计规则非常模糊，所以我们需要那种基本上能在没有一套会计准则的情况下照样干活也自在的人。于是他们就把我派过去了。我当时就在这么一个地方——“你需要有人在账上挪钱，或者去教堂”？听起来糟透了。

turns.en: They sent me over. You want a little loose accounting? Yes, if you don't need a bunch of rules. Do whatever you want. And so I ended up at this tech startup. It was a second time founder. He had done ad.com and sold it to AOL. And he was basically trying to recreate the same thing for video.
turns.zh: 他们把我派过去了。“你想要松散一点的会计吗？”“好啊，只要不需要一堆规则，随便你怎么搞。”于是我进了一家科技初创公司。创始人是二次创业，他之前做过 ad.com，卖给了 AOL。他基本上是想在视频领域复制同样的事。

turns.en: And so we raised a whole bunch of money from a whole bunch of people that I work with now. And the long and short story is we went bankrupt in like three and a half years. We're very early to something that seems like very obvious now. But out of that, I decided that we had done so much stuff that I thought was very simple.
turns.zh: 所以我们从一大堆人手里融了一大笔钱——其中很多人我现在还有合作。长话短说，我们大概三年半就破产了。我们进入得太早，做的是一件现在看起来非常明显的事。但从那段经历里，我意识到我们做了很多事情，我觉得本来是很简单的、

turns.en: And that we could like have avoided. And so I started a fractional CFO business. I thought I'd be a fractional CFO forever. I went to Babson because I was told if you don't know what to do when you're an adult, you get an MBA. And so the CFO of the company that I was at had gone to Babson in 1972.
turns.zh: 本来是可以避免的。所以我做起了兼职 CFO（fractional CFO，按比例外包的首席财务官）生意。我以为自己会一辈子做兼职 CFO。我去读 Babson 是因为有人告诉我，成年人要是不知道自己要干什么，就去读个 MBA。而我当时那家公司的 CFO 是 1972 年从 Babson 毕业的。

turns.en: And he was like, I will write your recommendation letter to Wharton. But only if you agree to go visit Babson. And honestly, as soon as I got to Babson, I knew it was the right fit. It's like a very special place. I had a very finance heavy background. And so doing more finance at Wharton didn't really make a ton of sense.
turns.zh: 他就说：“我可以给你写去 Wharton 的推荐信，但前提是你答应去 Babson 看一看。”说真的，我一到 Babson 就知道这里适合我。那是个非常特别的地方。我本身金融背景很重，所以再去 Wharton 读更多金融，其实没太大意义。

turns.en: I think I just like had heard that was the place to go. Whereas Babson, you know, allowed me to really think more creatively. And I started helping out with the endowment because as I just shared, I have a lot of venture background in terms of like my operating background. And just sort of fell in love with it.
turns.zh: 我觉得我只是听说那是大家公认该去的地方。而 Babson 让我可以更有创造力地去思考。我开始帮忙打理捐赠基金，是因为正如我刚才说的，从运营经历来看我有很多风险投资方面的背景。然后我就这么爱上了这件事。

turns.en: Very weird sequence of events. Babson had been largely volunteer run up into that point. They had brought on one individual in 2016. This is now 2018 that I came around. And they were sort of tugging along. There's around $420 million about halfway through my program. The gentleman that they had brought on left to start a fund of funds.
turns.zh: 接下来是一连串非常离奇的事。在那之前，Babson 基本上是靠志愿者在运作。他们在 2016 年请了一位专职人士，而我出现的时候是 2018 年，他们算是勉强撑着，规模大概 4.2 亿美元。到我 MBA 读到一半的时候，那位他们请来的先生离职去创立一家母基金（fund of funds）了。

turns.en: And ultimately, Babson came to me and said, would you like to take over the endowment? You can start right now. You have 24 hours to decide if you would like this job. And that was on March 13th of 2020. So there was like a few things happening in the world that ultimately, at the time, I was like, can I have my own business?
turns.zh: 最后 Babson 来找我，说：“你愿意接手这个捐赠基金吗？你可以马上开始。你有 24 小时决定要不要这份工作。”那是 2020 年 3 月 13 日。当时世界上正在发生一些事情……所以我当时的想法是：“我能不能保留自己的公司？

turns.en: I'm not going to do this forever. I'll help you out. And then it was actually my husband who was like, you're wildly underqualified to run an endowment. What an incredible opportunity like you should say yes to that. What planet are you on? And I can share more about why Babson was comfortable doing that.
turns.zh: 我不会一辈子做这个，我先帮你们一把。”结果真正推我的是我先生，他说：“以你的资历来管一个捐赠基金，简直差得太远了。这可是个不可思议的机会，你就该答应。你到底活在哪个星球上？”关于 Babson 为什么放心把这事交给我，我可以再多讲一点。

turns.en: We had extremely competent alumni support that helped me until I got up and running. But it really was such like a serendipitous. I mean, I never, if you had asked me even where the venture capitalists got their money before they gave it to us. When I was at that startup, I wouldn't have been able to tell you.
turns.zh: 我们有非常能干的校友支持我，一直帮到我把摊子转起来。但这真的完全是机缘巧合。我是说，如果你在我还在那家初创公司的时候问我，风险投资人的钱是从哪儿来的、然后才给到我们——我根本答不上来。

turns.en: So it was not like on my list of jobs I would do post-graduation. But so I spent the second year of my MBA getting up to speed on the endowment. And I've been there ever since. That's amazing. That's like a wild ride. That's like a movie. So before we get into kind of like your experience in jumping in and getting up to speed.
turns.zh: 所以这份工作压根不在我毕业后的求职清单上。总之我用了 MBA 的第二年把捐赠基金这套东西摸熟，然后就一直在做，到现在。太厉害了。这简直是一趟狂野之旅。这跟电影一样。那么，在我们深入聊你如何临危受命、快速上手之前——

turns.en: Could you give us the background on the Babson endowment like the history of it and being volunteer led and having very capable alumni helping? Yes. So the Babson endowment has been around a long time. But I would say in earnest, they got really serious about like how can we grow this portfolio of assets starting in about 2009.
turns.zh: 能不能给我们介绍一下 Babson 捐赠基金的背景，比如它的历史、一直由志愿者主导、以及有很能干的校友帮忙？好。Babson 捐赠基金已经存在很久了。但我会说，真正认真地开始思考“我们怎么把这盘资产做大”，是从 2009 年前后开始的。

turns.en: And at that time, the endowment was around $200 million. So tiny, tiny. And quite honestly, private equity came about because one of the investment committee members had worked at a fund of funds. He was at HarborBest and knew the industry very well.
turns.zh: 那时候捐赠基金大概只有 2 亿美元，非常非常小。说实话，私募股权（private equity）这块之所以做起来，是因为投资委员会里有一位成员曾在一家母基金工作过，他在 HarborBest 待过，对这个行业非常了解。

turns.en: And he said, you know, I think we have access that the people we're working with don't have, right? They're coming to us and asking for intros. People don't know this about Babson, but it's very sneaky in the LP world. You look at any big LP institution. There's a Babson alumni there.
turns.zh: 他说：“我觉得我们手里有一些资源，是我们合作的那些人没有的，对吧？他们反过来找我们，请我们帮忙引荐。”大家不太了解 Babson 的这一点，但它在 LP 圈子里其实非常“悄无声息地无处不在”。你看任何一家大型 LP 机构，里面都有 Babson 的校友。

turns.en: And so they really kind of saw this opportunity to like get into what at the time was kind of the next generation of up and coming venture funds.
turns.zh: 所以他们确实看到了一个机会，可以打进当时正在崛起的下一代新锐风险投资基金。

turns.en: And it was such a small portion of such a small pool of capital that they thought if we take really big swings here in a measured way, we can grow the assets to be more on par with our peers rather than having to focus on like chasing people for donations. And Babson does have a wonderful donor base, but it's also a very small school.
turns.zh: 而且这块只占一个非常小的资金池里非常小的一部分，所以他们想：如果我们在这里有节制地大幅出手，就能把资产规模做到跟同行更接近，而不必把精力都放在追着人募捐款上。Babson 确实有很棒的捐赠人基础，但它也是一所非常小的学校。

turns.en: And it's a relatively new school compared to like Harvard, you know, it's only about a hundred years old. So I think what's unique about Babson that enabled us to do that is you can only get a business degree at Babson. So everybody on the investment committee that's an alumni has some sort of finance background.
turns.zh: 跟 Harvard 这样的学校比，它算是相当年轻的，只有大约一百年历史。所以我觉得 Babson 独特、也让我们能做到这一点的地方在于：在 Babson 你只能拿商科学位。因此投资委员会里所有校友成员都有某种金融背景。

turns.en: And so they really did like a phenomenal job running this up until 2016 when they start to bring some of it in house. What they did was they have an investment committee, which is run by the Board of Trustees. They select the members of the investment committee based on like asset specific skills.
turns.zh: 在 2016 年开始把一部分工作收归内部之前，他们把这块做得非常出色。他们的做法是：设立一个由董事会（Board of Trustees）主管的投资委员会，并按资产类别的专业技能来挑选投资委员会成员。

turns.en: So we have about 15 people on our investment committees, big, big committee, but it's been really great for decision making at a high level. They manage all the public assets. I mean, they're responsible for the total endowment, but they retain discretion and always have over the portfolio.
turns.zh: 我们的投资委员会大约有 15 个人，是个非常非常大的委员会，但这在高层决策上真的很有帮助。他们管理所有公开市场资产。我是说，他们对整个捐赠基金负责，而且一直保留对组合的最终裁量权。

turns.en: We work with a consultant who helps on the public side. And then they established this sort of subcommittee, if you will, of the investment committee called the private equity committee, which we still have a version of today.
turns.zh: 我们聘请了一家顾问机构在公开市场这边提供帮助。然后他们在投资委员会下面设立了一个类似小组委员会的机构，叫私募股权委员会（private equity committee），今天我们仍然有一个版本在运作。

turns.en: So anything that my team does where we're bringing a recommendation to the investment committee comes with a yes or no stamp of approval from this advisory board, which is the private equity committee. And that has obviously evolved over the years, you know, at one time they were making all the decisions.
turns.zh: 所以我们团队任何要提交给投资委员会的建议，都会先带上这个顾问委员会——也就是私募股权委员会——“同意或不同意”的章。这个机制这些年当然也在演变，有一段时间所有决策都是他们做的。

turns.en: Now they're more of like an advisory role, but it's been such an incredible thing for the school. A lot of smaller endowments will ask me for advice on how to recreate this. And it's one of those things where like I think Babson just has something very special that would be very hard to recreate from scratch.
turns.zh: 现在他们更多是顾问角色，但这对学校来说是一件非常了不起的事。很多规模更小的捐赠基金会来向我请教怎么复制这套机制。而这件事我觉得 Babson 拥有某种非常特别的东西，从零开始复制会非常难。

turns.en: It's like when people say, how do we become Silicon Valley? And it's like, I don't know Atlanta. It's a very special set of circumstances. It's like, can I have to start like this? That's fascinating. Did you hear any of the sort of backstory of how everybody came to agree they were going to swing for the fences?
turns.zh: 就像有人问“我们怎么变成 Silicon Valley”，然后回答是“我不知道，Atlanta 呗”——那是一组非常特殊的条件凑在一起的结果。“那我能不能也从这样开始？”这太有意思了。你有没有听过一些背景故事，就是大家当初是怎么达成一致、决定要全力挥棒博大的？

turns.en: Like you've got folks representing all these different asset classes. And the Fund of Funds guy with the venture role of X is the one who gets to make the big bets. That's a fascinating room to be part of. And I just wonder, you know, have you heard anything about what that process was like? Yeah, it was very slow and steady.
turns.zh: 你想想，屋子里坐着代表各种不同资产类别的人，而那位做过母基金、有风投履历的人，才是负责下重注的那个。能在那样的房间里待着一定很有意思。我只是好奇，你有没有听说过当时那个过程是什么样的？有，那是一个非常缓慢、稳扎稳打的过程。

turns.en: And this is something that I think institutions have gotten wrong in the past that Babson did very well. It's like we went into it with a clear picture of like these are the people around the table who have really good access. In a perfect world, these are the names that we would want to be in.
turns.zh: 这一点我觉得是很多机构过去做错了、而 Babson 做得很好的地方。我们一开始就有很清晰的图景：桌上这些人手里有非常好的资源，如果一切理想，我们最想进的就是这些名字。

turns.en: We can deal with the fact that we're $500,000 check later. Like let's just figure out how can we get into one of these names. And we literally went one at a time. And even today the portfolio is very concentrated and that was an intentional decision. But it started really small. Like now we're a 25% target for private equity.
turns.zh: 至于我们只能开 50 万美元的支票，那是后面的事，先想办法挤进其中一个名字再说。我们真的是一家一家地推。即便到今天，这个组合依然非常集中，那是有意为之的决定。但它起步非常小。比如现在我们对私募股权的目标配置是 25%。

turns.en: But they didn't take 25% of 200 million and say like we should ram this into venture as fast as possible. Right, like that. It's sort of evolved very slowly of like what are we comfortable with? One of the the co-chair of my IC likes to describe this as like steering the Titanic.
turns.zh: 但他们并没有拿 2 亿的 25% 说“我们要尽快把这些钱全砸进风投”。不是那样的。这是一个慢慢演变的过程：我们能接受到什么程度？我们 IC 的一位联席主席喜欢把这形容成“开泰坦尼克号”。

turns.en: Like bad analogy and that Babson's obviously not the Titanic. But like you are making very small like a big ship, right? Every other boat did not say anything. Any boat besides the Titanic. Wait, wait, did I miss something? What happened at the end? We're just steering a big ship. A big ship. Right.
turns.zh: 这个比喻很烂，而且 Babson 显然不是泰坦尼克号。但就像开一艘大船，你的转向幅度必须非常小，对吧？其他船都没说什么。除了泰坦尼克号之外的任何船。等等等等，我是不是漏了什么？最后到底发生了什么？我们只是在开一艘大船。一艘大船。对。

turns.en: So we just want to go like nice and slow, right? Like no over corrections one way or another. Take a little bit of a turn, see where we are, reevaluate. Like we're shuffling our feet, right? And that's I think the approach that they took and honestly like that's still how my team approaches going into new areas of the portfolio today.
turns.zh: 所以我们就是想走得又稳又慢，对吧？不要往任何一个方向过度修正。稍微转一点，看看我们在哪儿，再重新评估。就像我们在一小步一小步地蹭，对吧？我觉得这就是他们当时采取的思路，说实话，直到今天我的团队进入组合的新领域时，用的还是这套方法。

turns.en: Because I think that's where people get into trouble, right? Is where they're like, oh my gosh, I'm behind. I didn't have a thesis on this. Everyone's making money in Web 3. How do I get into all the Web 3 funds, right? Like that's not the way to do venture and Babson was clear on that from the jump.
turns.zh: 因为我觉得人就是在那儿出问题的，对吧？就是那种“天哪，我落后了，我对这个赛道没有投资论点（thesis），所有人都在 Web 3 上赚钱，我要怎么才能进所有的 Web 3 基金？”——那不是做风投的方式，而 Babson 从一开始就很清楚这一点。

turns.en: How much do you think that can be contributed to having such an informed finance based investment committee? Because I've had recent conversations with a number of organizations, large allocators that are rebuilding or starting over starting from scratch.
turns.zh: 你觉得这在多大程度上要归功于有一个这么懂行、金融背景这么强的投资委员会？因为我最近跟不少机构聊过，一些大型配置方（allocator）正在重建、或者干脆从零开始重做

turns.en: They're venture portfolio and hearing the team that focuses on private equity and is on the ground and venture capital have to like play these essentially games with convincing their investment committee who's just like, hey, we haven't made any money in this. And we heard it's really scary and risky.
turns.zh: 自己的风险投资组合。听那些专注私募股权、真正在风投一线的人说，他们基本上得跟自己的投资委员会玩各种“说服游戏”，而委员会的态度是：“嘿，我们在这上面没赚到过钱，而且我们听说这东西很吓人、风险很大，

turns.en: So we need to just get into these six names. And it's like, yes, pretty hard to get into those six names and not get sent to their like secondary and tertiary funds first, right? So how much do you like, you know, how much is it aligned from that success from just like having such an informed investment committee?
turns.zh: 所以我们只需要进这六家名字就行。”可现实是，想进那六家名字非常难，而且你多半会先被推给他们的二期、三期基金，对吧？所以你觉得，这份成功有多少是来自“有一个这么懂行的投资委员会”？

turns.en: A couple of things. I think the sophistication and the trust that comes from our investment committee is invaluable. Obviously, I've only ever been an LP at Babson, so I did not appreciate like how good I had it until I kind of was in this for a few years and started to understand other people's investment committees.
turns.zh: 有几方面吧。我觉得我们投资委员会的专业度和信任是无价的。显然，我只在 Babson 做过 LP，所以在入行几年、开始了解别人的投资委员会之前，我根本没意识到自己的处境有多好。

turns.en: I think we have to keep in context to the timing of when this was right like 2009 was a very different market environment. And the public markets were not necessarily like the most attractive asset class in the world.
turns.zh: 我觉得还得放在当时的时间点上看，2009 年是非常不一样的市场环境，公开市场那时候未必是世界上最吸引人的资产类别。

turns.en: It's also worth noting that our current IC chair has been involved with the endowment and has been like really instrumental in its growth since 2009. So that makes a huge, huge difference, right? That continuity.
turns.zh: 还有一点值得提：我们现在的 IC 主席从 2009 年起就一直参与捐赠基金，对它的增长起到了非常关键的作用。这种延续性带来的差别是巨大的，对吧？

turns.en: And he's like a pretty incredible thinker in terms of risk like he was clear from the beginning of like the pool of money is $200 million. Obviously, we're not supporting a huge portion of the operating budget at that size.
turns.zh: 而且他在风险方面的思考相当出色。他从一开始就很清楚：这笔钱的池子是 2 亿美元，以这个体量，我们显然并不支撑运营预算的很大一部分。

turns.en: So what benefit is it to me to not to like avoid risk when this is a long term pool of capital, you know, I don't want to risk a huge portion of the capital. But if we are saying we have an outsized information advantage here, why would we not try to get the school like a leg up and lean in?
turns.zh: 那么，当这是一笔长期资金的时候，一味规避风险对我有什么好处？我当然不想拿一大笔钱去冒险。但如果我们说自己在信息上有超常的优势，那为什么不去为学校争取一个先发优势、大胆压上去呢？

turns.en: And so I think this is true of CIOs, of investment committees. It's like all about the team that you have around the table and their philosophy and the goals of the institution, right?
turns.zh: 所以我觉得这对首席投资官（CIO）、对投资委员会都一样：关键在于坐在桌子周围的这支团队、他们的理念，以及机构的目标，对吧？

turns.en: If that's not a huge liquidity demand, they couldn't have taken this risk, but they're a small school that was running really well and like they what the goal was, how do we scale the assets, not how do we keep liquidity around so that we can fund the operating budget.
turns.zh: 如果流动性需求不是特别大，他们本来也承担不了这种风险。但他们是一所运转得非常好的小学校，目标是怎么把资产规模做大，而不是怎么留着流动性去支撑运营预算。

turns.en: And so I think there's so many things that come together for like a perfect storm. But the fact that I can go to my investment committee and have like a great conversation about venture today, venture 10 years from now and they still understand and feel like it's worth it to put dollars into their consistently is a huge advantage.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得是很多事情凑在一起，形成了一场“完美风暴”。但直到今天，我还能跟我的投资委员会好好聊一聊当下的风投、十年后的风投，而他们依然理解，并且觉得持续往里投钱是值得的——这是一个巨大的优势。

turns.en: Right? Like, you know, it's, that's the whole game. If you try to time it and only be in the right things at the right time, you'll never do it, right?
turns.zh: 对吧？这就是整个游戏的关键。如果你想择时，只想在对的时间进对的东西，你永远不会成功的，对吧？

turns.en: So are there any things that you could recommend to other smaller endowments? Is there a tactic or just something that you've been able to share with friends that is not so unique to Bebson? Yeah, I think there's a number, like I think that what I just highlighted about like being consistent over been to this is important like that.
turns.zh: 那么，有没有什么建议可以给其他规模较小的捐赠基金？有没有什么打法、或者你分享给朋友的东西，是并不那么“Babson 独有”的？有，我觉得有好几条。比如我刚才强调的“保持持续投入”，这一点很重要。

turns.en: I think even if that means you're doing less dollars, like if you're budget is smaller and you're maybe not at the comfort level that we are where we do, you know, a significant amount every year, like picking partners that you really value and believe in and then backing them consistently.
turns.zh: 我觉得哪怕这意味着投的钱更少——比如你的预算更小，还没到我们这种每年投出一大笔的从容程度——那么挑出你真正看重、真正相信的合伙人，然后持续地支持他们，

turns.en: Is going to yield far better results than like chasing who has the best returns right now. I would also say and maybe like a word of caution that like the dispersion of returns is very real, right? So if you are going to go into this and be like, we can get into some pretty good stuff.
turns.zh: 带来的结果会远好于去追“眼下谁回报最好”。我还要说一句提醒：回报的离散度（dispersion of returns）是真实存在的。所以如果你进场时的想法是“我们能进到一些不错的基金”，

turns.en: Like you're going to be disappointed. I think you have to go into it with a point of view and like a real clear plan on how you're going to access who you believe is the best.
turns.zh: 那你多半会失望。我觉得你必须带着自己的观点进场，并且有一套非常清晰的计划：你要怎么去接触到你认为是最好的那批管理人。

turns.en: Because otherwise, like the liquidity premium just isn't worth it quite frankly. I mean, you'd be better off even if you wanted to do privates, you'd be better off in like the lower middle market on the buyout front.
turns.zh: 否则坦白讲，那点流动性溢价（liquidity premium）根本不值。我是说，即便你想做私募，你还不如去做中小市场下端（lower middle market）的并购（buyout）。

turns.en: So I think it's just being really thoughtful. What I would discourage everyone not to take it negative, but like take it negative. I think that the thing that people get wrong the most frequently, if they see headlines like SpaceX and Anthropic and they're like, oh my gosh, we're not in those.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得就是要非常审慎。有一点我会劝大家——不是要往负面想，但确实要往负面想：人们最常犯的错，就是看到 SpaceX、Anthropic 这样的头条，然后想“天哪，我们没投到这些，

turns.en: We should put money in those now. Like no, you should have put money in those eight years ago. You're too late, right? Like that's why I say I think you have to make a clear thesis, be thoughtful about how you're going to approach it and then slowly execute that thesis over time.
turns.zh: 我们现在就该把钱投进去”。不，你八年前就该投了，你已经太晚了，对吧？所以我说，你必须有一个清晰的论点，想清楚自己打算怎么切入，然后用时间去慢慢执行这个论点。

turns.en: You should not say, I heard this now, it made 20% year on year in venture. So I need venture now, right? Like that's a recipe for disaster. I understand how you would have an unfair advantage in understanding kind of like all the way down, sorry, upstream with like the actual companies and kind of assessing that.
turns.zh: 你不应该说“我刚听说风投去年同比涨了 20%，所以我现在需要风投”，对吧？那是灾难配方。我能理解，为什么你们在一路往上游、也就是对实际公司层面的理解和判断上，会有一种“不公平的优势”。

turns.en: But then you're skipping kind of a step because now you need to underwrite the people who underwrite said company. So how did you come up to speed on that?
turns.zh: 但那样你其实是跳过了一个环节，因为现在你需要去承保（underwrite，即尽调并押注）那些承保这些公司的人。那你在这方面是怎么快速上手的？

turns.en: So a couple of things. I had been working with the endowment team for about 18 months before they made this decision. So the whole volunteer committee knew me, they knew how I thought I was familiar with the portfolio. Like was I ready to be in charge yet? Probably not. But like it was, I wasn't brand new out of nowhere.
turns.zh: 有几方面。在他们做这个决定之前，我已经跟捐赠基金团队合作了大约 18 个月。所以整个志愿者委员会都认识我，知道我怎么思考，我也熟悉这个组合。要说我当时准备好独当一面了吗？大概还没有。但我绝不是一个凭空冒出来的新人。

turns.en: I think the underwriting piece of it actually came very naturally to me. I think because so much of it is understanding like the relationships and the people and how they think about the companies, I actually felt like it was easier to underwrite the funds than it was on a company by company basis.
turns.zh: 我觉得承保判断这件事对我来说其实来得很自然。因为它很大程度上是在理解关系、理解人、理解他们怎么看这些公司，所以我甚至觉得给基金做承保判断，比一家一家公司去判断更容易。

turns.en: I mean, I worked in technology, but I am by no means a technologist. I like struggled to explain what videology did until the day I left. So like I was it, it wasn't like I had some great engineering background where I could be helpful.
turns.zh: 我是说，我在科技行业工作过，但我绝不是一个技术专家。我到离职那天都还讲不清楚 Videology 到底是干什么的。所以并不是我有什么了不起的工程背景能帮上忙。

turns.en: I think I just knew enough people that I could get good referencing done. I knew who people liked, who people didn't like. I knew who like had lost a lot of money and who had not.
turns.zh: 我觉得只是因为我认识的人够多，能把背景调查（referencing）做得扎实。我知道大家喜欢谁、不喜欢谁，知道谁亏了很多钱、谁没亏。

turns.en: And so that was very helpful. I think it allowed me to get the learning curve very fast. I also think the fact that I was an accountant made it very easy for me to understand not only like the financial dynamics of companies in the portfolio, but also like I didn't have to spend time learning how to read the financial statements for the funds and all of that came very quickly as well.
turns.zh: 这一点非常有帮助，让我学习曲线走得很快。我还觉得，会计出身让我很容易理解组合里公司的财务动态；而且我不用花时间去学怎么读基金的财务报表，这些东西我也上手很快。

turns.en: So in that sense, I think everyone was really comfortable. What took a lot of reps and I like will scream this from the rooftops forever was the discretion and like the discernment that comes with deciding what managers to back is something that there is no shortcut for like I joined Babson in 2020.
turns.zh: 从这个意义上说，我觉得大家当时都挺放心的。真正需要大量重复练习的——这一点我会永远站在屋顶上大喊——是决定押注哪些管理人时所需的那种裁量权和 discernment（识别判断力），这件事没有捷径。我是 2020 年加入 Babson 的。

turns.en: We didn't do a net new manager that I chose until January of 2023. So and I probably take like even still today somewhere between 300 and 500 calls a year.
turns.zh: 直到 2023 年 1 月，我们才做了第一笔由我挑的全新管理人（net new manager）。而且即便到今天，我一年大概还要接 300 到 500 通电话。

turns.en: So the first like year and change was just reps and reps and reps meeting people building my reputation, getting Babson's brand out there because that was still very new as well. You know, at the time I joined, we were like a $2 million check and the endowment has more than doubled in size since then.
turns.zh: 所以头一年多就是在不停地练：见人、建立自己的口碑、把 Babson 的品牌打出去，因为那时候这也还是非常新的。你知道吗，我加入的时候，我们一张支票大概 200 万美元，而现在捐赠基金的规模已经翻了一倍多。

turns.en: So that there's a lot that comes with that that I think they saw a lot of value in my operator background to be able to build an investment office and then I also think it was a level of comfort that I had given that I come from startup land that like everything wasn't laid out perfectly and we were kind of figuring it out as we went.
turns.zh: 这背后伴随的东西很多。我觉得他们非常看重我的运营者背景，能借此搭建一个投资办公室；另外我想也因为我来自初创圈，对于“一切都没有完美地铺好、我们边做边摸索”这种状态，我本身就适应得很自在。

turns.en: Now we're going to take a quick break to speak with our sponsor. On the show today, we have our stellar partner and industry expert Shane Galley, leader of Sidley's venture funds practice and now host of the podcast talk BC. We highly recommend you listen.
turns.zh: 现在我们先休息一小会儿，跟我们的赞助商聊几句。今天来到节目的是我们出色的合伙人、行业专家 Shane Galley，他是 Sidley 风险投资基金业务的负责人，现在也是播客 Talk BC 的主持人。我们强烈推荐你去听。

turns.en: You have extensive experience also representing limited partners and because plenty of listening to the show, I was curious what's top of mind for you right now when it comes to LP's participation in venture.
turns.zh: 你在代表有限合伙人（limited partners）方面也有丰富的经验，而且我听了你不少节目，所以我很好奇：眼下关于 LP 参与风险投资，你最关心的是什么？

turns.en: Again, that tends to be LP by LP dependent somewhat because each one has its own, you know, touch points and sensitive spots just on the, you know, the intake part of it.
turns.zh: 这个还是要看具体的 LP，因为每一家都有自己的关注点和敏感点，哪怕只是在“准入”这个环节上。

turns.en: Look, I think from an LP's perspective, the commodity they're buying is the people that they're investing in and so there just is a much greater diligence going on with respect to team. You know, relative performance record by the individual managing directors. You know, what does generational planning look like at your firm?
turns.zh: 你看，我觉得从 LP 的角度来说，他们买的“商品”就是他们要投的这些人，所以在团队方面的尽职调查（diligence）就要深入得多。比如各位董事总经理（managing directors）各自的相对业绩记录，再比如你们公司的代际规划（generational planning）是什么样的？

turns.en: Because LP's smartly when they go to make an investment in these funds, they don't think about it just the fun, the instant fund, it's the next three funds. The questions, I don't want to have to think I should have asked a question in fun one when I can ask it and wait till fun three.
turns.zh: 因为 LP 很聪明，他们在投这些基金的时候，想的不只是当下这一支，而是接下来的三支。至于那些问题——我不希望到时候才后悔“这个问题我在第一支基金就该问”，所以现在就要问，而不是等到第三支基金。

turns.en: I want to start to investigate what it looks like to be an LP for you over the course. So that's talking about what your distribution plan looks like. How does the team view performance? How do you measure performance? What again generational planning is a huge thing?
turns.zh: 我想开始研究一下，在长期过程中做你们的 LP 是什么体验。这就要谈到你们的分配（distribution）计划是什么样，团队怎么看待业绩、怎么衡量业绩，还有——代际规划，这也是件大事。

turns.en: So, you know, what are the, the diligence going on in particular from the institutional side now is just more than it ever has been. And that's driven by, obviously, the underlying realization that the people you're investing in are the team.
turns.zh: 所以现在，尤其是机构这边做的尽调，比以往任何时候都要多。驱动这一点的，显然是那个根本认知：你投的就是这支团队。

turns.en: But, you know, you got a lot of regulatory and diligent stuff going on on your own side, whether it's ESG or, you know, there are certain industries that you can't invest in because you're a govern sovereign.
turns.zh: 但你自己这边也有很多监管和尽调方面的事情，不管是 ESG，还是说因为你是主权基金（sovereign），某些行业你就不能投。

turns.en: You know, so some of it is just, it's really investor dependent. But the themes are, you know, do I have an out if something happens to like the key person provision or a no fault division or a GP removal or those are the kinds of things that I think LPs find comfort in.
turns.zh: 所以有些东西确实要看具体的投资人。但主题是共通的：万一出事，我有没有“出口”——比如关键人条款（key person provision）、无过错“离婚”条款（no-fault divorce）、或者罢免 GP（普通合伙人）。我觉得这些正是让 LP 感到安心的条款。

turns.en: And so there's been a lot of investigation and a lot of conversation around the human elements of these deals. And then obviously you get into what is the investment strategy look like and then the management fee obviously is a huge issue.
turns.zh: 所以围绕交易中的“人的因素”，有大量的调查和讨论。然后自然会谈到投资策略是什么样，接着管理费（management fee）显然是个大问题。

turns.en: You know, and then when funds are talking about like tiered carry, well, you know, what is historical performance look like. So some of it is also very fund dependent.
turns.zh: 然后当基金谈到分层附带权益（tiered carry）时，那历史业绩又是什么样？所以有些内容也非常取决于具体是哪支基金。

turns.en: The two key things, LPs always, it's people you're investing in and it's the damn economics. And if we can kind of find some satisfaction somewhere in there on a lot of the stuff. And if the fund manager is receptive to a lot of the particular areas, whether it's confidentiality or use a name or I got a transfer to an affiliate or I got this weird investment restriction that I got to live by or I need to be able to transfer my interest if you invest in a gambling company or whatever it is, right.
turns.zh: 对 LP 来说永远有两个关键点：一是你投的人，二是那要命的经济条款（economics）。如果我们能在很多细节上找到某种程度的满意，如果基金管理人在很多具体领域愿意接受——不管是保密、能不能使用名称、我要把权益转让给关联方、我得遵守某个奇怪的投资限制、或者如果你投了一家博彩公司我需要能转让我的权益，诸如此类，对吧。

turns.en: I just think it's LPs now more than ever looking for true partnership. And as I counsel my GPs, I think when I was a much younger lawyer, I tended to be a little more rock and sock and robots. And this was a negotiation. And by God, my guys were going to win and you guys were going to lose. That's all gone.
turns.zh: 我只是觉得，LP 现在比以往任何时候都更在寻找真正的伙伴关系。我在给我的 GP 做顾问时常说，我年轻时当律师，往往更“硬碰硬”——这是一场谈判，老天在上，我的人要赢，你们的人要输。那一套现在全没了。

turns.en: It's just like, look, your job is to help them create a great partnership. You're not always going to agree on everything, which you can be respectful about it in the way in which you kind of have those conversations. And, you know, because your job is to help them create a great partnership. The last thing in the world to form a really solid bedrock for a fun one is to have a bunch of unhappy LPs because you jerked them around in the fundraising. I mean, that's not the way you move through the world to get this thing on the right tracks to start.
turns.zh: 就是说，你的工作是帮他们缔造一段伟大的合伙关系。你们不可能在所有事情上都一致，但你在进行这些对话时可以保持尊重。因为你的工作就是帮他们缔造伟大的合伙关系，而给一支首期基金（fund one）打下坚实根基时，最糟糕的事就是在募资过程中把 LP 耍得团团转、留下一堆不开心的 LP。我是说，那样做事，你根本没法让这件事一开始就走上正轨。

turns.en: And it took some while to get that kind of mentality and approach. But I think that that the LPs side, and I don't do a ton of it. But, you know, the stuff that I do has made me appreciate the LPs position and what it's like to be an LP and one of the really, really big fun or an emerging fund. And how should you behave, you know, as an LP?
turns.zh: 要形成这种心态和做法，也花了一些时间。但我觉得 LP 这一侧——虽然我做的量不算大——我做的这部分让我更理解 LP 的处境，理解做一个 LP 是什么感觉，尤其是在一支真正很大的基金或者一支新兴基金里，作为 LP 你应该怎么做。

turns.en: And because I know what GPs feel for how LPs, you know, do that work. And, you know, so it keeps us abreast as to not just from terms and, you know, all kind of market standard stuff and what does LP have to say about this that, you know, there. But, you know, what are LPs thinking? You know, what's important to them? And a lot of that can also happen. I mean, I go to my GPs annual meetings. And so, you know, I talk to a lot of LPs about this kind of stuff because it's important.
turns.zh: 也因为我知道 GP 对 LP 做这些事是什么感受。所以这让我们不只是紧跟条款、紧跟各种市场标准做法、紧跟“LP 对这条怎么说”，还能知道 LP 在想什么、什么对他们重要。很多事情也是这么发生的——我会去参加我的 GP 客户的年会，所以我会跟很多 LP 聊这类事情，因为这很重要。

turns.en: So, yeah, that's the kind of stuff that, you know, the LP work has shown me and allows us to, you know, give some kind of perspective on. And since the team is so important to the LPs, are there any interesting stories you can share of a transition or a succession situation that, you know, could give us some color?
turns.zh: 所以，是的，这就是 LP 这块工作让我看到的东西，也让我们能提供一些视角。既然团队对 LP 这么重要，有没有什么关于交接或继任（succession）的有意思的故事可以分享，给我们一点具体的画面感？

turns.en: Ooh, yeah. Okay. So, I had a succession planning. It was the main issue in this, in this fund. So, LP comes a very large institutional P, you know, fundraising. Let's just call it in the range of 400 to 600 billion somewhere in there.
turns.zh: 哦，有。好。我遇到过一次继任规划，它是这支基金里的核心问题。有一家非常大的机构 LP 参与募资，我们就说规模在 4000 亿到 6000 亿这个区间吧。

turns.en: And this was not a fund one. Obviously, this was like a fund for, I think this one was. But the cycle between funds has been like five years.
turns.zh: 而且这显然不是一支首期基金，我想这一支应该是第四期。基金之间的周期大概是五年。

turns.en: So, there's been some time between fund one and fund four so that the GPs who were around and fund one were kind of more gray hair-ish and, you know, but old state guard venture valley people who had, you know, been around since dinosaurs walking around the earth here.
turns.zh: 所以从一期到四期中间过了不少时间，一期时候就在的那些 GP 已经更多是白发苍苍的了——那些老派的风投圈老人，可以说从恐龙还在地球上溜达的时候就在这行了。

turns.en: So, this fund four comes online and, you know, they look at the key person provision. And the team is now, at that point, it was probably like seven or eight people. Instead of the prior fund, it was three. Maybe four got at it.
turns.zh: 于是第四期基金启动，他们看关键人条款。那时候团队大概有七八个人，而上一期只有三个人，最多算四个。

turns.en: So, the team's just much bigger. The two principal founding partners are now in their late 60s. And so, because they raised their first fund when they were a little older, they were, you know, in their 20s, they were in their early 40s.
turns.zh: 所以团队大了很多。两位主要的创始合伙人现在已经六十多岁快七十了。因为他们募第一支基金的时候年纪就偏大——不是二十多岁，而是四十出头。

turns.en: So, you know, the LP's kick tires on that a lot. And the old founding partners did not want to hear it. We're not going to budge with respect because they were the two key people in all the funds and no one else had ever had their name on the key person provision.
turns.zh: 所以 LP 在这件事上反复盘问。而两位老创始合伙人不想听这些：“我们不会让步”，因为在所有基金里关键人都是他们俩，从来就没有别人的名字出现在关键人条款上。

turns.en: And, you know, a couple of LPs walked because of it. And after a while, after some slow fundraising parts of it. And, you know, frankly, just some very honest discussion internally as a team with us about what market has, you know, what does a transition plan look like. So, it's just the great part about this firm is they were very receptive to a very bad set of initial circumstance.
turns.zh: 结果真有两家 LP 因为这件事走掉了。过了一段时间，加上募资进展缓慢，坦白说，还有团队内部跟我们进行的一些非常坦诚的讨论——市场怎么看、交接计划应该长什么样。这家公司最可贵的一点是，面对一开始非常糟糕的局面，他们非常愿意接受意见。

turns.en: And they went about and thought about what it meant because, you know, if the best way you can lip mistest is a GP. What people think about your firm is to like have somebody walk away because of what you're doing. And, you know, these were, these were LPs that were in funds one and fund two.
turns.zh: 他们开始认真思考这意味着什么。因为，作为一家 GP，最能毁掉别人对你公司看法的方式，就是有人因为你的做法而转身离开。而这些走掉的 LP，是投过一期和二期基金的 LP。

turns.en: So, they were not brand new customers coming to the door. These were existing LPs. So, they were people who were well familiar with kind of the team and teaming. And it just became something that created I think ultimately a lot of positivity. So, like two other people then became part of the key person provision.
turns.zh: 所以他们不是刚上门的新客户，而是现有的 LP，是非常熟悉这个团队和团队运作方式的人。这件事最终反而带来了许多正面的结果：后来又有了另外两个人被纳入关键人条款。

turns.en: And there was some a lot of generational planning stuff that went on in the management company entity. Like people were starting to be admitted and, you know, like exit packages were starting to be negotiated. And so sometimes, you know, the LP relationship can be a kickstarter from that perspective. So, I think, you know, that was one very, very interesting. And it happened over time. But it was one just sort of exemplary way in which the whole thing was going to be.
turns.zh: 管理公司主体层面也做了大量代际规划的工作，比如开始有人被吸纳进来，退出方案（exit packages）也开始谈判。所以有时候，LP 关系从这个角度看反倒成了一个“启动器”。我觉得这是一个非常非常有意思的案例，它是随时间慢慢发生的，但整个过程堪称典范。

turns.en: Because it could have gone the other way. Because you could have just said, I'm going to put a flame throw to this place. We're not raising this fund. We're going to just manage out whatever we got and, you know, hell or high water, damn you all.
turns.zh: 因为事情完全可能走向另一个方向。你本来可以说：“我要把这地方一把火烧了，这基金我们不募了，手上有什么就管到什么程度，不管发生什么，你们都见鬼去吧。”

turns.en: You know, to their credit, they just understood that this was about more than them at this point. And, you know, it took a little while to get there. And it took a few kicks in the butt. But, you know, it was fun to be able to counsel through that as well. And not just on their side, but on the younger partner side and the kind of be part of that room and have them ask you what you're doing.
turns.zh: 值得称赞的是，他们明白到这个阶段，这件事已经不只是关于他们自己。要走到那一步花了一些时间，也被“踢了几脚”。但能陪着他们走过这段顾问过程也很有意思——不只是在他们这一侧，也在年轻合伙人那一侧，能身处那个房间，让他们来问你该怎么做。

turns.en: Ask you what your opinion is and what have other clients done and how of things may have been managed. So, you know, that was a very fascinating transaction to say the least.
turns.zh: 问你的看法，问别的客户是怎么做的、事情是怎么处理的。所以说，那至少是一笔非常有意思的交易。

turns.en: Thank you for joining us on the show, Shane. If you're a GP or LP looking for expert guidance on fund formation and venture capital legal matters, you can visit Sidley's website, S-I-D-L-E-Y dot com. And now back to our LP interview.
turns.zh: 谢谢你来到我们的节目，Shane。如果你是 GP 或 LP，正在寻找基金设立和风险投资法律事务方面的专业指导，可以访问 Sidley 的网站 sidley.com。现在我们回到 LP 访谈。

turns.en: Well, speaking of State State, what is sort of the, what is the lay of the land today? And what do you spend your time looking for to compliment that?
turns.zh: 那么说到当下的局面，今天这块“地形”是什么样的？为了与现有组合互补，你把时间花在寻找什么上面？

turns.en: Yes, I said so. I mentioned when I started, we're about 420 million. Today we're about 910 million. So, very different landscape. Still, yes, it's very exciting. It's great, great for the school. Still 25% target. So, my team is managing about $300 million, just like the long and short of it.
turns.zh: 是的，我说过，我接手的时候大概是 4.2 亿，今天大约是 9.1 亿，所以格局非常不同了。但这依然很令人兴奋，对学校来说是极大的好事。私募股权的目标配置仍然是 25%，所以长话短说，我的团队管理着大约 3 亿美元。

turns.en: 70% of that, roughly, a little more, is in venture. And then about 30% of that, little less, is in lower middle market buyout. So, the way we're structured is our public portfolio is really set up to absorb a lot of the risk that we're taking on the private side.
turns.zh: 其中大约 70%、还多一点，投在风险投资上；大约 30%、略少一点，投在中小市场下端的并购。我们的结构是这样的：公开市场组合的设计，本来就是为了吸收我们在私募一侧承担的很多风险。

turns.en: We've sized the allocations for that to be the case. And we're taking big swings, right? Big swings within reason.
turns.zh: 我们在设定各类资产配置（allocation）比例时就是照这个来的。我们在大幅挥棒，对吧？在合理范围内大幅挥棒。

turns.en: And so, from that standpoint, like the venture overweight makes a lot of sense. It's also the reason that we focus on the lower middle market when we look at buyout because it's a slightly riskier, slightly higher return profile. Same is true with growth equity. We kind of do that opportunistically. Honestly, we don't have a ton of it.
turns.zh: 所以从这个角度看，超配（overweight）风投是非常合理的。这也是我们看并购时聚焦中小市场下端的原因，因为那是风险略高、回报也略高的特征。成长股权（growth equity）也是一样，我们是机会主义地做，说实话量并不大。

turns.en: But we're really looking for like the highest return profile we can find in every asset class and we categorize everything under private equity. So, today we have, you know, probably we have 18 manager relationships, 13 of those are active.
turns.zh: 但我们真正在找的，是每个资产类别里能找到的最高回报特征，而且我们把所有这些都归在私募股权这个大类下。今天，我们大概有 18 个管理人关系，其中 13 个是活跃的。

turns.en: I think the right number of names is probably somewhere between like 15 and 16. And we are actively working on adding a little bit more buyout into the portfolio.
turns.zh: 我觉得合适的名字数量大概在 15 到 16 家之间。我们正在积极往组合里增加更多并购。

turns.en: Not because we don't believe in venture. We very much believe in venture. More because our venture portfolio is way more mature than our buyout portfolio, given that's where we started.
turns.zh: 不是因为我们不相信风投，我们非常相信风投；更多是因为我们的风投组合比并购组合成熟得多——毕竟那是我们起步的地方。

turns.en: And we just have some like concentration risk we have to manage. So, last year and a half, I would say my team spent a lot of time in lower middle market buyout. We'll probably add two net new names there, I would say. And then the third spot, you know, is always open because we want to stay as opportunistic inventor as possible.
turns.zh: 而且我们也有一些集中度风险需要管理。所以过去一年半，我的团队在中小市场下端并购上花了很多时间，我觉得我们大概会在那里新增两个全新的名字。而第三个位置永远空着，因为我们希望尽可能保持机会主义。

turns.en: In terms of what we look for, I have like the worst answer to this. I swear it is very much like I know it when I see it. And it's like the word GPs get hate that answer. It's fair. It's like it's so ambiguous. That's the realist answer though. It's not personal. It's like, it's not you.
turns.zh: 至于我们在找什么，我给的答案大概是最糟糕的那种。我发誓，真的就是“我看到就知道”。GP 们最恨这个答案，这我理解，因为它太模糊了。但这确实是最真实的答案。这不是针对谁，不是说“你不行”。

turns.en: And there's so many things that come into it. Like you had said, Alexa, everybody's a nine out of 10. And it's so true. It's like you meet all these incredible people. And we try to look at it through, we have like a four pillar framework. So we're looking at, and this is nothing revolutionary.
turns.zh: 里面有太多因素在起作用。就像你说的，Alexa，每个人都是十分里的九分。这话太对了，你会遇到一堆了不起的人。我们试着通过一个框架来看——我们有“四大支柱”框架，我们看的是（这没什么革命性的）：

turns.en: But we're looking at team track record strategy. And then the last piece is what like kills half the stuff. And that's Babson fit. And so like when you meet these people, right, like most people have an incredible team. You don't like go out and raise a venture fund.
turns.zh: 团队、过往业绩（track record）、策略。而最后一块，是能砍掉一半项目的那个——Babson 契合度（Babson fit）。所以你见这些人的时候，绝大多数人都有非常出色的团队。你不会随随便便就出去募一支风投基金，

turns.en: If people don't like you and you're not amazing and you haven't done cool stuff for the most part, right. And then like the strategy piece, we actually don't take a huge stance on strategy one way or the other. We run like a concentrated high conviction playbook. But we have both in our portfolio.
turns.zh: 如果人们不喜欢你、你也不够出色、大体上也没做过什么厉害的事，对吧。然后在策略这一块，我们其实不会在策略上采取强烈立场，不管哪个方向。我们跑的是集中、高信念（high conviction）的打法，但两种策略我们组合里都有。

turns.en: We tend to skew away from larger fund sizes simply because of the dynamic I just mentioned about the outsized return and the small pool of capital. But what we really end up boiling things down to is like, how does what this person or people are going to bring compliment what already exists here.
turns.zh: 我们倾向于避开规模较大的基金，纯粹是因为我刚才提到的那个动态：资金池很小，却要求超额回报。但我们最终把事情归结到的核心是：这个人或这些人能带来的东西，如何与我们这里已有的东西互补。

turns.en: And that is a much harder decision making framework than where we started, which was like, we need more exposure. And so that piece of it gets very tricky. And we're not looking for completely separate networks. And we're certainly not looking for totally overlapping networks.
turns.zh: 这比我们起步时的决策框架难得多，那时候就是“我们需要更多敞口”。所以这一块会变得很棘手。我们既不是在找完全不相干的人脉网络，当然也不是在找完全重叠的网络。

turns.en: So we try to think about like the pre-seed seed series a little bit of series B. How do we want to cover that and where do we have white space? And who do we believe is the best in that white space? And outside of that, like in terms of sectors and stuff, we are big believers and the managers are going to take us where we're still.
turns.zh: 所以我们会去想：pre-seed（种子前）、seed（种子期）、series A，再加一点 series B，我们想怎么覆盖这些阶段，哪里还有空白地带（white space），以及我们认为谁在那片空白里是最强的。除此之外，在行业这些方面，我们非常相信“管理人会带我们去该去的地方”。

turns.en: And that's what we're supposed to be. Like that's what the two percent is for. If I was smart enough to know that myself, I would just do it.
turns.zh: 而这正是我们本来就该扮演的角色。那 2% 的管理费就是干这个用的。如果我自己聪明到能知道该投哪儿，那我干脆自己去做就好了。

turns.en: And so that's kind of our philosophy. Few exceptions to that rule, right? Like life sciences, you know, you should probably specialize in that. But like for the most part, we're not in the business of saying like, I believe the world is going here.
turns.zh: 这大概就是我们的理念。当然这条规则有少数例外，比如生命科学（life sciences），你大概应该专精于此。但大体上，我们做的不是那种“我认为世界会往这个方向走，

turns.en: How do I find the best manager there? We are more like, how do I find the best manager? And where do they think the world is going? That's very similar to as hitting almost 12 years in the business and starting out as a specialist, realizing finding the best and the most.
turns.zh: 我怎么找到那儿最好的管理人”的事。我们更像是：我怎么找到最好的管理人，以及他们认为世界在往哪走？这跟我在这行快 12 年、从专才（specialist）起步的经历非常相似——我意识到，找到最好的、最有

turns.en: The best founders who could potentially bring alpha, it's usually not because I thought of this amazing thesis and made up a market map. Sorry associates, if you still exist. But it's really about finding great founders and then being able to show you something that seems so obvious yet you never kind of like really saw it.
turns.zh: 可能带来 alpha（超额收益）的创始人，通常不是因为我想到某个了不起的投资论点、画出一张市场地图（market map）。抱歉了各位 associate（投资经理），如果这个岗位还存在的话。它真正靠的是找到伟大的创始人，然后他们能给你看一样东西，看起来如此显而易见，可你却从来没真正看见过。

turns.en: And so that makes sense that you all would feel the same way. For you've been in the business now for a while and we've had a lot of cycles and mini cycles that have happened. How have you and your team been able to stay up to speed and understanding where the trends are going in the business?
turns.zh: 所以你们有同样的感受完全说得通，因为你们入行也有一段时间了，而这中间经历了很多大周期和小周期。你和你的团队是怎么保持跟上节奏、理解这个行业趋势走向的？

turns.en: Yeah, so my team full time is me and one other gentleman, Luis. And like speak very transparent, we work a lot. I think like the nuts and bolts of how we stay up to speed. But I think like the biggest thing for us that we try to focus on is being like intellectually flexible, curious about what's happening in the market open-minded.
turns.zh: 是这样，我的全职团队就是我加上另一位先生 Luis。说得很透明一点：我们工作量非常大——这是我们能跟上节奏的具体做法。但我觉得我们努力聚焦的最重要的一点，是保持思维上的弹性，对市场上正在发生的事保持好奇，保持开放。

turns.en: I think this is like the biggest thing for institutions that invest in venture is like it's so easy to be like that will never work. We try to approach everything from like let's assume this is going to work. What are we missing here?
turns.zh: 我觉得这是投资风投的机构最重要的一课：说“那玩意儿永远成不了”太容易了。我们试着对每件事都从这个角度切入：“假设它会成，那我们漏掉了什么？”

turns.en: And I think that allows us to just be a little bit more open to the magic that comes out of venture versus like looking for everything that's wrong with it. So in terms of like we're obviously reading everything, you know, I get 5,000 news letters a day. It's like all we can do to like my inbox is a really scary place.
turns.zh: 我觉得这让我们更能接纳风投里冒出来的“魔法”，而不是只盯着它哪里不对。至于阅读，我们显然什么都读，我一天能收到 5000 份 newsletter。我们能做的也就是……我的收件箱是个很吓人的地方。

turns.en: But like it's you know that I think we're doing all the things everyone else is doing of like following the news cycle. I think the trick is like what are the people that we believe are the smartest around us to actually think of this and how should we interpret it?
